newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq and U.N. implement oil sales plan.
newsitem.headline: Iraq and U.N. implement oil sales plan.

text.p: Iraq was free early on Tuesday to sell limited oil exports and return to world petroleum markets for the first time since sanctions were imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

The long-delayed plan, which allows Baghdad to sell oil in order to buy food, medicine and other necessities for its people suffering under sanctions, went into effect at 12:01 a.m. EST (0501 GMT). The United Nations gave Iraq the go-ahead on the plan on Monday.
No one is certain when the oil will actually flow. Some Iraqi officials say it will start immediately but others suggest a day or so is more realistic.
Under the so-called oil-for-food plan, concluded in May but held up by disputes over implementation, Iraq will be able to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy the humanitarian goods.
Security Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy called it "the largest humanitarian operation ever launched by the United Nations in the world."

Speaking to reporters after notifying council members that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali had given the final go-ahead, he said: "More than 20 million innocent Iraqi civilians will be finally saved from starvation and untold suffering."

Both the oil sales and the purchase of humanitarian supplies are subject to close U.N. monitoring. If all goes well, the Security Council may renew the deal when the initial six months expire. But council members say there is no chance it will be increased after three months.

In Washington, State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies stressed that the agreement did "not signal an end or the first step toward the end of the sanctions regime against Iraq, against (President) Saddam Hussein's regime."

A prime condition for the full lifting of sanctions, which includes a ban on normal oil sales, is word from the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of disarming Iraq that all its weapons of mass destruction have been scrapped.
The head of the commission, ambassador Rolf Ekeus, is now on one of his periodic visits to Baghdad, trying to account for Iraq's arsenal of SCUD missiles.

In giving the green light, Boutros-Ghali, a constant negotiator in the operation since he took office five years ago, said: "This is a victory for the poorest of the poor of Iraq, for the women, the children, the sick and the disabled. I hope the humanitarian dimension will always prevail in the work of the United Nations."

The U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) has said 4,500 children under the age of five were dying each month from hunger and disease while the U.N. World Food Programme estimated about 180,000 children under five were malnourished.
Iraq will be able to export slightly under 600,000 barrels of oil a day, according to current prices. It exported over 3 million barrels a day before the Gulf War.
The proceeds will be placed in an escrow account in the New York branch of the Banque Nationale de Paris.
Some $1.32 billion of each $2 billion from the oil sales will go for humanitarian supplies, including $260 million earmarked for goods for the largely Kurdish-populated north.

Of the remainder, $600 million will be funnelled into a U.N. compensation fund to pay Gulf War reparations. Another $20 million will go to the U.N. weapons commission while administrative and operational costs account for the rest.
